title: Dengue in children (India)
specialty: Paediatrics / Infectious Diseases / Paediatric Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Dengue in children in India: case categories, warning signs, outpatient care, weight-based fluid resuscitation for warning signs and shock, haematocrit-guided decisions, blood product thresholds and discharge, built on the ICMR Dengue Fever STW (October 2019) with paracetamol dosing from the ICMR Fever in Children STW. The adult Dengue (India adaptation) topic covers adults.
findings: Case categories, warning signs, investigations, outpatient care (paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs, daily PCV and platelets), crystalloid bolus 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes in shock, 10 mL/kg/hour for warning signs, the stepwise taper (10, 7, 5, 3 mL/kg/hour) stopping at 48 hours, platelet transfusion below 10,000/cumm or with bleeding, red cell and FFP indications and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR Dengue STW (October 2019).
Paracetamol 15 mg/kg from the ICMR Fever in Children STW.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR Dengue STW is not child-specific; the mL/kg regimens are used for children as written.
Paracetamol interval and daily maximum are not given in the ICMR workflows (usual practice 4–6-hourly, no more than 60 mg/kg/day).
The ICMR flowchart lists some rate ranges without clear sequence; the main sequence is shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus infection with yearly epidemics across India. Most children have a febrile phase of 2–7 days with fever, myalgia, rash and headache. Around defervescence, a critical phase of increased capillary permeability can cause plasma leakage, rising haematocrit, pleural effusion, ascites and shock, sometimes with bleeding and organ involvement. Warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, liver enlargement over 2 cm) identify children who need hospital care (ICMR STW). Careful, haematocrit-guided fluid therapy prevents both shock and fluid overload; platelet transfusion is rarely needed. The danger window is the 24–48 hours around defervescence: a child whose fever settles may look better while plasma leaks silently, so a falling temperature is a reason to look harder, not to discharge. Infants, obese children and those with secondary infection are at higher risk of severe dengue.
keyMechanisms: Viral infection and immune activation increase vascular permeability.
Plasma leakage causes haemoconcentration, effusions and hypovolaemic shock.
Reabsorption of leaked fluid in recovery risks fluid overload.

symptoms: Headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash (ICMR STW)
Restlessness, lethargy or reduced urine output (impending shock)
physicalSigns: Liver enlargement over 2 cm (warning sign) (ICMR STW)
Weak rapid pulse, pulse pressure under 20 mmHg, cold clammy skin (shock) (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Shock: weak rapid pulse, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension (ICMR STW)
Respiratory distress from fluid accumulation, impaired consciousness (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Secondary infection with a different serotype

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever with chills, pallor and splenomegaly in an endemic area; a positive smear or rapid diagnostic test settles it.
Prominent, often disabling polyarthritis with less thrombocytopenia and no plasma leak; chikungunya IgM or PCR settles it.
Eschar, lymphadenopathy and raised transaminases in the monsoon; scrub typhus IgM ELISA settles it.
Gradually rising fever over a week, abdominal pain and relative bradycardia; blood culture settles it.
Exposure to flood water, calf pain, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice and kidney injury; leptospira IgM settles it.
Toxic child with a focus, high white count and early shock without haemoconcentration; blood culture and procalcitonin help settle it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Fever plus two of: nausea or vomiting, rash, myalgia, headache, retro-orbital pain, arthralgia, haemorrhagic manifestations, in an endemic area.
Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, liver over 2 cm, or features of shock.
Fluid accumulation with respiratory distress, severe bleeding or impaired consciousness.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: NS1 positive (days 1–5) or IgM positive (after day 5)

clinicalManagement.title: No warning signs
actions: Paracetamol for fever; avoid NSAIDs (ICMR STW).
Oral fluids; daily clinical review with PCV and platelets (ICMR STW).
Admit if any warning sign appears.

clinicalManagement.title: Warning signs
actions: Ringer's lactate or normal saline 10 mL/kg/hour (ICMR STW).
Reassess at 1–2 hours with PCV; if improving taper 10, 7, 5 and 3 mL/kg/hour; stop by 48 hours (ICMR STW).
Not improving or PCV rising at reassessment: increase Ringer lactate to 15 mL/kg/hour, then colloid 10 mL/kg/hour, reassessing hourly (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Shock
actions: Crystalloid or colloid 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes (ICMR STW).
Reassess HR, RR, BP, PCV hourly; if PCV rising give further fluid or colloid 10–20 mL/kg; if PCV falling with instability suspect bleeding and transfuse (ICMR STW).
Look for and treat anaemia, acidosis and myocardial dysfunction (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Blood products
actions: Platelets below 10,000/cumm or prolonged shock or massive bleeding (ICMR STW).
Packed cells for overt blood loss of 10% or more of blood volume or refractory shock (ICMR STW).
FFP or cryoprecipitate for coagulopathy with bleeding (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge
actions: No fever for 48 hours, rising platelets, stable PCV without IV fluids, observed 24 hours after stopping fluids (ICMR STW).
Explain warning signs to parents and the need to return at once if abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding or lethargy appears (usual practice).

vignette.text: Riya, a 9-year-old girl from Delhi weighing 28 kg, is brought in October on day 5 of illness. Her fever settled this morning, but she now has abdominal pain, has vomited four times and is lethargic. Pulse is 128/min, BP 100/86 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds and the liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Haematocrit is 46% (it was 38% two days ago) and platelets are 38,000/cumm.

guidedApproach.title: Leak, not bleeding, is the main problem
guidedApproach.prompt: Why do children with dengue go into shock as the fever settles?
guidedApproach.guidance: Dengue virus infects monocytes and endothelium, and the host immune response — stronger in secondary infection with a different serotype — releases cytokines that make capillaries leaky. During the critical phase around defervescence plasma leaks into the pleural and peritoneal spaces, the haematocrit rises and circulating volume falls. Children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so the pulse pressure narrows before the BP falls; hypotension is a late sign. Thrombocytopenia is common but bleeding is usually minor unless shock is prolonged, when acidosis and coagulopathy develop. After 24–48 hours the leak stops and fluid is reabsorbed, so continuing IV fluids causes overload.

guidedApproach.title: Warning signs and early shock
guidedApproach.guidance: Classify each child. Dengue without warning signs can be managed at home with daily review. Warning signs — abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, liver enlargement over 2 cm, and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets — mean admission. Look for compensated shock: tachycardia, cool peripheries, capillary refill over 2 seconds and a pulse pressure under 20 mmHg, even with a normal systolic BP. Severe dengue includes shock or respiratory distress from fluid accumulation, severe bleeding and organ impairment such as hepatitis, encephalopathy or myocarditis.

guidedApproach.title: Use the haematocrit to steer fluids
guidedApproach.prompt: What do the tests tell you?
guidedApproach.guidance: NS1 antigen confirms dengue in the first 5 days and IgM after day 5, but treatment does not wait for confirmation. A baseline haematocrit taken early in the illness is the reference point: a rise of 20% or more indicates plasma leak (WHO), while a falling haematocrit in an unstable child suggests concealed bleeding. Check haematocrit before and after each fluid bolus and every few hours during resuscitation. Platelets guide transfusion only when below 10,000/cumm or with bleeding. Chest X-ray and ultrasound show effusions and gallbladder wall oedema; liver and kidney function and albumin show organ involvement. Always test for malaria and other co-infections.

guidedApproach.title: Fluid that is enough, but not too much
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you give fluids in dengue with warning signs and shock?
guidedApproach.guidance: For warning signs without shock give Ringer lactate or saline 10 mL/kg/hour, reassess at 1–2 hours with the haematocrit and, if improving, taper to 7, 5 and 3 mL/kg/hour, stopping by 48 hours; if not improving, increase to 15 mL/kg/hour and then colloid 10 mL/kg/hour. For shock give 20 mL/kg crystalloid over 15 minutes, then reassess heart rate, BP, perfusion and haematocrit; if the haematocrit is still high, repeat crystalloid or colloid 10–20 mL/kg; if it falls while the child is unstable, suspect bleeding and give packed red cells 10 mL/kg. Use paracetamol 15 mg/kg for fever and avoid NSAIDs, aspirin and IM injections. Give platelets only below 10,000/cumm, in prolonged shock or with massive bleeding.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 9-year-old girl on day 5 of dengue has abdominal pain, repeated vomiting and lethargy. Her fever settled this morning. Pulse 128/min, BP 100/86 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds. Haematocrit has risen from 38% to 46% and platelets are 38,000/cumm.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best immediate management?

options.explanation: Platelets are given only below 10,000/cumm, in prolonged shock or with major bleeding (ICMR STW).

options.text: Oral fluids and discharge as fever has settled
options.explanation: The narrow pulse pressure and rising haematocrit show compensated shock in the critical phase.

options.text: Crystalloid 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes, then reassess with haematocrit
options.explanation: Correct. A pulse pressure under 20 mmHg with poor perfusion is shock; give a 20 mL/kg bolus and reassess (ICMR STW).
NSAIDs are avoided in dengue because of bleeding and kidney risk (ICMR STW).
This is a tapering rate, far too little for shock.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Narrow pulse pressure is shock even with a normal systolic BP.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy with dengue shock received two crystalloid boluses of 20 mL/kg. He remains tachycardic with cold peripheries. His haematocrit has fallen from 48% to 36% and he has had a dark, tarry stool in the last hour with little urine since. Platelets are 22,000/cumm.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most likely problem and next step?

options.text: Ongoing plasma leak; give colloid 20 mL/kg
options.explanation: A falling haematocrit in an unstable child points to bleeding, not leak.

options.text: Concealed bleeding; transfuse packed red cells 10 mL/kg
options.explanation: Correct. A falling haematocrit with persistent shock suggests bleeding needing blood (ICMR STW).
He is still in shock, so diuretics would worsen perfusion.
Myocarditis is possible, but the haematocrit fall and melaena point to bleeding first.
Platelets alone do not replace lost red cells or restore circulation.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Unstable with a falling haematocrit: think bleeding and transfuse.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 6-year-old girl was admitted with dengue warning signs and has received IV fluids for 52 hours. Her fever has gone for 2 days, platelets are rising and she now has puffy eyelids, a respiratory rate of 40/min and new bilateral crackles. Haematocrit is 32%.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate step?

options.explanation: She is not in shock; more fluid would worsen overload.
Platelets are rising and there is no bleeding.

options.text: Start antibiotics for pneumonia and continue fluids
options.explanation: The picture is reabsorption of leaked fluid, not infection.
Colloid adds volume to an already overloaded circulation.

options.text: Stop IV fluids, monitor closely and seek senior review for a diuretic if she stays stable
options.explanation: Correct. Fluids should stop by 48 hours; in the recovery phase reabsorption causes overload (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise fluid overload in the recovery phase.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Stop IV fluids by 48 hours; recovery brings reabsorption.

patientEducation: Return at once for abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness or cold hands.
lifestyleAndDiet: Remove stored water; use nets and repellents.
mdtReferrals: Higher centre or PICU for severe dengue
dischargeCriteria: Rising platelets, stable PCV without IV fluids (ICMR STW)
Good appetite and urine output, no respiratory distress (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Daily review in the febrile and critical phases; review after discharge if symptoms recur.

algorithms.title: Child with suspected dengue: fluid decisions

nodes.text: Child with fever 2–7 days and suspected dengue
Shock: weak rapid pulse, pulse pressure under 20 mmHg, cold clammy skin or hypotension?
Crystalloid 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes; check PCV before and after
Reduce to 10 mL/kg/hour, then 7, 5, 3 mL/kg/hour as vitals and PCV improve; stop by 48 hours
Breathlessness, crackles, puffy eyelids or effusions in recovery (fluid overload)?
Stop IV fluids; senior or PICU review; diuretic only if haemodynamically stable
Discharge when afebrile 48 hours, platelets rising and PCV stable off fluids
Repeat crystalloid or colloid 10–20 mL/kg; correct acidosis, calcium, glucose; consider inotropes
Suspect concealed bleeding: packed red cells 10 mL/kg; blood products if coagulopathy
Any warning sign (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, liver over 2 cm)?
Admit: Ringer lactate 10 mL/kg/hour, reassess at 1–2 hours with PCV
Taper 7, 5, 3 mL/kg/hour over the next hours; stop by 48 hours
Ringer lactate 15 mL/kg/hour, then colloid 10 mL/kg/hour; reassess hourly; treat as shock if it develops
Oral fluids, paracetamol, no NSAIDs; daily review with PCV and platelets; return if warning signs
